title: Pages, tuples and heap files
goal: By the end, you can explain why a database that changes data in place cuts each table into pages of a fixed size, read one PostgreSQL page byte by byte, say how a page keeps rows of any length behind slot numbers that never change, and build a page that inserts, deletes and tidies itself.
opening:
Picture your phone telling you its storage is full. You delete 2,000 old photos, check again, and the bar hasn't moved. The photos went to an album called Recently Deleted, where they wait in case you change your mind.

A database can surprise you the same way. The team behind a coffee-shop payments app deletes a year of old payments, millions of rows, to free disk space. The next morning, the table's file is exactly as big as before.

It's easy to expect a delete to erase. That's what deleting a file does, and the rows really are gone from every answer the database gives. But inside the file, their bytes are still there.

In Bytes, pages and durability, our store kept one file that only grew, plus every key in memory. A table of a billion rows needs a different design. In this lesson, we'll cut a table's file into pages, read one page byte by byte, and follow a deleted row until its space comes back. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: PostgreSQL gives each row an address: the page it's on, and its slot number inside that page. A row sits at (0,4), page 0, slot 4. You delete the rows in slots 2 and 3 of the same page, then run `VACUUM`, the command that cleans up deleted rows. What is the row's address now?
options: (0,2), because the rows after the gap move up to fill it
Still (0,4): VACUUM may move the row's bytes inside the page, but never its slot number
Somewhere on a new page, because VACUUM moves rows off pages that have holes
Every address changes, because VACUUM rewrites the whole table file
warmup.why: Indexes, the lookup structures that find rows fast, store the address (page, slot), so the slot number must not change while the row lives. VACUUM tidies the page by moving row bytes and updating the slot's note of where the row starts. In the Try it below, the row in slot 4 moves from byte 8000 to byte 8096 and stays in slot 4. The first option is the tempting one, and it's exactly what would break every index. The last option describes `VACUUM FULL`, which rewrites the table into a new file and locks everyone else out while it works. Plain VACUUM doesn't.

sections.h: Cutting a table's file into 8 KB pages
sections.body:
Picture a table that lists every payment a busy payments app has ever taken: a billion rows, far more than fit in memory. The store from Bytes, pages and durability kept every key in memory, so it can't hold this one. And a table needs more. Rows get changed and deleted. And an index must be able to point at a row and find it again later. An index is a lookup structure that finds a row by a value, such as its id, without reading everything. This lesson starts the second family of storage engines from that lesson: the kind that keeps data in pages of a fixed size and changes them where they lie. So let's start from scratch. How should rows sit in a file?

First, the words. A table is a named set of rows, like one sheet of a spreadsheet, and each column has a name and a type. Our running example is a `ledger` table, a list of money moving in and out of accounts, one row per movement. Each row has an `id`, an `account` name and an amount in cents. (Whole cents add up exactly, while a computer's decimal fractions sometimes don't.)

The hardware answers the first part of the question. Drives and the kernel, the core of the operating system, move data in blocks, never single bytes; the previous lesson showed blocks of 4 KB and 16 KB. So a database cuts every table file into fixed-size **pages**, and always reads and writes a whole page. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, uses pages of 8 KB, 8,192 bytes. Page 0 is bytes 0 to 8,191 of the file, page 1 the next 8,192 bytes, and page `n` always starts at byte `n × 8192`. To read one row, PostgreSQL reads its page. The page is also what the cache in the next lesson holds.

Insert 1,000 small ledger rows into a new PostgreSQL table and look at its file: 57,344 bytes, exactly 7 pages. PostgreSQL stores each table as its own file under its data directory, the folder where the server keeps everything (`base/<database id>/<file number>`), and grows it one page at a time. A table over 1 GB (about a billion bytes) is split into several files of 1 GB, but it's still one numbered row of pages.

Now every row can have an address: which page, and which row inside that page. PostgreSQL calls it the **ctid** and writes it `(page, item)`, where the item is the row's number inside its page. `(0,1)` is the first row on page 0. In the Try it, rows 1 to 157 fill page 0, and row 158 starts page 1 at `(1,1)`. An index stores that address next to each value (lesson 4 of this track builds one). So a row's item number must not change while the row stays on its page, or every index entry that points at it breaks. The figure shows the picture for this lesson: a numbered row of pages, and inside each page a list of slots that point at rows.

PostgreSQL's table file is a **heap**: rows go wherever there's room, in no particular order. That raises a practical question. Which page has room for the next insert? Checking every page of a 100 GB table, 13 million pages, for each insert is out of the question. So PostgreSQL keeps a small side file, the **free space map**, that records roughly how many free bytes each page has. An insert asks it for a page with enough room. Only when no page has room does PostgreSQL add a new page at the end of the file. You'll see it work in the third Try it, when a new row lands in space freed on page 0 instead of on a new page 7.

Every row of our ledger is the same small size, so the rows pack neatly. Real rows aren't so polite. Next, we'll fit rows of different lengths into one page, and keep the promise that their addresses never change.

try.title: Find a table's pages
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`. Docker runs programs in containers, each with its own private view of the computer, and this command starts PostgreSQL 18 in one. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's small program where you type commands and read the answers: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Predict: 1,000 rows of three small columns. How many 8 KB pages?

Paste the block below. `CREATE TABLE` makes the table, and `generate_series(1, 1000)` makes the numbers 1 to 1,000, one row each. The second query takes the page number out of each row's ctid and counts the rows on each page. The last line runs `ls -l`, which lists a file with its size, inside the container.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
Seven pages: 157 rows on each of pages 0 to 5, and 58 on page 6. Row 157 is `(0,157)`, and row 158 is `(1,1)`:

```text
       file       | bytes
------------------+-------
 base/16384/17600 | 57344

  ctid   | id  | account | amount_cents
---------+-----+---------+--------------
 (0,1)   |   1 | acct-1  |          100
 (0,2)   |   2 | acct-2  |          200
 (0,157) | 157 | acct-7  |        15700
 (1,1)   | 158 | acct-8  |        15800
```

The file number (17600 here) differs on your machine. `ls -l` shows the same 57,344 bytes. The next sections explain why exactly 157 rows fit.

sections.h: Rows of different sizes in one page: the slotted page
sections.body:
Rows have different lengths. A ledger row for account `acct-1` takes 48 bytes; one with a 500-letter note takes over 500. So how do we place them in an 8 KB page, and find row 4 again quickly?

Version 1 packs them back to back from the start of the page. To find row 4, read row 1's length and skip it, read row 2's length and skip it, and so on. That's slow, but it works until we delete row 2. Then we either leave a hole, which every later walk must recognise and skip, or slide rows 3 onwards down to close it. Sliding moves every one of those rows to a different offset, a different count of bytes from the start of the page. An index that noted where row 3 was is now wrong.

Version 2 puts a small array, a numbered list, at the start of the page. Entry 4 holds row 4's offset and length, so finding it is one lookup, and a row can move as long as its entry is updated. But how big is the array? A fixed size caps the number of rows per page. And if the rows start right after the array, the array can't grow without moving every row.

Version 3 lets the two grow toward each other. A filing drawer shows the idea. Picture a drawer of folders with a numbered list taped inside the front: line 4 says where folder 4 sits. When you pull two folders out and push the rest together, you correct the positions on the list, but line 4 is still line 4. Anyone who noted "drawer 0, line 4" still finds the folder. In a page, the drawer is the page, the list is an array of slots, and each folder is a row. This is the **slotted page**. PostgreSQL uses it, and so do SQLite, a small database that lives in a single file and runs inside most phones, and Oracle, a database many large companies pay for. A slotted page has four parts:

- a small header at the start of the page,
- an array of slots right after it, one per row, each holding the row's offset and length (PostgreSQL calls a slot a **line pointer**),
- the rows themselves, packed from the end of the page backwards,
- free space in the middle.

The drawer picture breaks on space. A list taped inside a drawer takes no room from the folders. On a page, the slots and the rows grow toward each other and compete for the same 8 KB.

The header keeps two offsets. `pd_lower` is where the slot array ends, and `pd_upper` is where the rows begin. An insert copies the row in right below `pd_upper`, adds a slot right after `pd_lower`, and moves both toward each other. The page is full when they would cross. Free space is always one gap in the middle, whatever sizes the rows have.

PostgreSQL's numbers, from its page layout docs, are a 24-byte page header, 4-byte line pointers, and an optional special area at the very end that table pages don't use. In the Try it, page 0 of `ledger` has `lower = 652` and `upper = 656`. That's 24 bytes of header plus 157 line pointers of 4 bytes, then 4 free bytes, then 157 rows of 48 bytes reaching to byte 8,192. The page is full: one more 48-byte row needs 52 bytes with its line pointer.

The slot array adds one step to every lookup: an index points at the slot, and the slot points at the row. What that step buys is one promise. **A row's slot number never changes while the row lives, even when its bytes move.** An index entry says "page 0, slot 4". The page can rearrange its bytes freely, as long as it updates slot 4's offset. The stepper shows this on the 4 KB page you build in the lab.

So a page can move its bytes around safely. Next, we'll delete a row and watch where its bytes go.

try.title: Read page 0 with pageinspect
steps: In the same psql session, predict `lower` and `upper` for page 0 from what you know: a 24-byte header, 157 rows, 4-byte line pointers and 48-byte rows.

Run the two queries below. pageinspect is an extension, an add-on that ships with PostgreSQL, for looking at raw pages, and this course's database turns it on when it starts. `get_raw_page` copies one 8 KB page, and `page_header` and `heap_page_items` turn its bytes into readable columns.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
```text
 lower | upper | special | pagesize
-------+-------+---------+----------
   652 |   656 |    8192 |     8192

 lp  | lp_off | lp_flags | lp_len | t_hoff
-----+--------+----------+--------+--------
   1 |   8144 |        1 |     48 |     24
   2 |   8096 |        1 |     48 |     24
   3 |   8048 |        1 |     48 |     24
 156 |    704 |        1 |     48 |     24
 157 |    656 |        1 |     48 |     24
```

`lower` is 24 + 157 × 4 = 652. Row 1 sits at the very end of the page, and each next row 48 bytes lower, until row 157 starts at 656, which is `upper`. `special = 8192` means the special area is empty. `lp_flags = 1` means the slot is in normal use. `t_hoff` is the size of each row's header, which the last section takes apart.

sections.h: Deleting a row: a mark now, the space later
sections.body:
Delete row 2 from a full page. What should happen to its 48 bytes?

The simplest answer is to remove them at once and slide the neighbours over the gap. PostgreSQL can't do that. A query that started before your DELETE must still be able to read row 2 until it finishes, so that every query sees the data as it was when it began. (MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM, lesson 4 of the Transactions track later in the course, explains why in full.) So the DELETE only writes a number into the row. Every change runs inside a transaction, a group of changes that becomes final all at once, and every transaction gets a number, its transaction id. The DELETE writes its id into the row's **`t_xmax`** field, which means "deleted by". Run `DELETE FROM ledger WHERE id IN (2, 3)` and look at page 0: rows 2 and 3 are still there, at the same offsets with the same length, with `t_xmax` set.

That's the surprise from the opening. The rows are gone from every answer, and their bytes are still in the file, like photos waiting in Recently Deleted.

The space comes back later, through **VACUUM**, PostgreSQL's cleanup command. You rarely run it by hand: a background helper called autovacuum runs it for you. Once no running query can still need the dead rows, VACUUM does two things you can see on the page:

1. The line pointers of rows 2 and 3 become unused: offset 0, length 0, `lp_flags = 0`.
2. The page is compacted: its live rows slide together, so the free space is one piece again. Row 4 moves from byte 8,000 to byte 8,096, right below row 1, and `upper` rises from 656 to 752. That's 96 more bytes of free space in one piece, two rows' worth.

Row 4 is still `(0,4)`. Its bytes moved and its slot didn't, which is the reason the slot array exists. And the table file is still 57,344 bytes. VACUUM makes space reusable inside the file. It gives space back to the operating system only when whole pages at the very end of the file are empty.

This is where the photo picture breaks. Emptying Recently Deleted frees room on your phone, while VACUUM frees room for new rows of the same table. That's usually what you want, because new rows will fill it. If you really need the disk back, `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table into a new file. It locks everyone else out of the table until it's done, though, so save it for a quiet hour.

Then insert a new row. It lands at `(0,2)`, in a slot VACUUM has freed. Reusing a slot number is dangerous: if an old index entry still said "page 0, slot 2", a lookup would find the new row instead of nothing. PostgreSQL reuses a slot only after VACUUM has removed every index entry pointing at it. This table has no index, so VACUUM could mark the slots unused straight away. With an index, a dead slot first waits in a dead state (`lp_flags = 3`) until the index entries are gone.

Your lab page is simpler and stricter. It has no VACUUM and no indexes to clean, so it never reuses a slot number. A deleted slot stays dead for the life of the page, and compaction moves bytes but leaves every slot where it is.

One number from the Try its still needs explaining: 48 bytes for a row that holds two numbers and a short name. Next, we'll take a row apart.

try.title: Watch VACUUM tidy a page
steps: Delete two rows and look at the first four slots. Predict before each query: what changes? `t_xmin` is the id of the transaction that inserted the row.
Run `VACUUM`, then look at the header and the slots again.
Check the file size, then insert one row and note its ctid. `RETURNING ctid` asks the INSERT to print the new row's address.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
After the DELETE, rows 2 and 3 are untouched except for `t_xmax`:

```text
 lp | lp_off | lp_flags | lp_len | t_xmin | t_xmax
----+--------+----------+--------+--------+--------
  1 |   8144 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
  2 |   8096 |        1 |     48 |    857 |    858
  3 |   8048 |        1 |     48 |    857 |    858
  4 |   8000 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
```

After VACUUM, `upper` is 752 (up from 656), slots 2 and 3 are empty, and row 4 has moved:

```text
 lp | lp_off | lp_flags | lp_len | t_xmin | t_xmax
----+--------+----------+--------+--------+--------
  1 |   8144 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
  2 |      0 |        0 |      0 |        |
  3 |      0 |        0 |      0 |        |
  4 |   8096 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
```

The file is still 57,344 bytes, and the new row comes back as `(0,2)`. Your transaction ids differ.

sections.h: What a row costs: its header, and where big values go
sections.body:
Two questions are left from the Try its. Why does a row holding two numbers and a 6-letter name take 48 bytes? And what happens to a row too big for an 8 KB page?

The figure takes row 1 apart. The first 24 bytes are the **tuple header** (PostgreSQL calls a stored row a tuple). That's 23 bytes of fields, plus one byte of padding: an unused byte that keeps what follows lined up. Three of the fields matter here. `t_xmin` is the transaction that inserted the row, and `t_xmax` the one that deleted or replaced it (0 if none). `t_ctid` is this row's own address, or the address of a newer version of it. The rest are flags. The columns follow. `id` takes 8 bytes. `'acct-1'` takes 7: a 1-byte length, then 6 letters. Then comes 1 byte of padding, so that `amount_cents` starts at an offset divisible by 8, and the amount takes the last 8 bytes. PostgreSQL lines up 8-byte values this way because the processor reads them in one step when they start at a multiple of 8.

So half of this row is overhead, and each row also costs a 4-byte line pointer. Narrow tables pay the most: a table of two `int` columns (whole numbers of 4 bytes each) spends 28 bytes per row on header and slot, before any data. Count it when you estimate how big a table will get.

Now the big row. The simplest idea is to let it spill over into the next page. That breaks the picture this lesson built: a slot can only point inside its own page, and reading one row could take several page reads. So a row must fit in one page. Your lab page is stricter still: it refuses any record bigger than a quarter of the page.

PostgreSQL keeps rows small with **TOAST** (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique). When a row is wider than about 2 KB, it works on the row's biggest values. First it tries to compress them, which means storing the same data in fewer bytes, for example by writing a long run of one letter once, with its count. If the row is still too wide, it moves values out into a separate TOAST table, cut into chunks of about 2,000 bytes (four fit on one page). The row keeps an 18-byte pointer to them. A single value can be up to 1 GB this way.

The Try it fills a `receipts` table with two long texts and shows both outcomes. A string of 20,000 copies of one letter compresses to 241 bytes and stays in the row. A string of 12,800 hexadecimal digits (0 to 9 and a to f) that look random barely compresses, so it moves out. The row on the page shrinks to 46 bytes (24 of header, 4 for the `int`, 18 for the pointer), and the text lives in seven TOAST chunks. Reading that column means reading those chunks too. `SELECT id FROM receipts` never touches them, while `SELECT *`, which asks for every column, does. That's one honest reason to name the columns you want.

That's also where today's design stops. A heap keeps rows in no order, so finding one payment by its id still means reading every page. And every query, quick or slow, reads pages, often the same ones again and again.

try.title: Push a value out to TOAST
steps: Create a table, then insert one long value that compresses well and one that barely compresses. `md5` turns any text into 32 hexadecimal digits that look random, and `string_agg` joins 400 of them into one string.
Predict which one stays in the row on the page.
Compare each value's length with its stored size (`pg_column_size`), look at the row lengths on page 0, then read the TOAST table's chunks.
When you're done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
```text
 id | chars | stored_bytes
----+-------+--------------
  1 | 20000 |          241
  2 | 12800 |        12800

 lp | lp_len
----+--------
  1 |    269
  2 |     46
```

Row 1 was compressed and stays in the page, 269 bytes with its header. Row 2 is a 46-byte stub that holds an 18-byte pointer. The TOAST table holds its text in chunks 0 to 5 of 1,996 bytes each and a last chunk of 824 bytes: 12,800 bytes in all.

compare.title: PostgreSQL heap page vs SQLite b-tree page

a.label: PostgreSQL heap page
a.title: 8 KB
a.src:
24-byte page header (pd_lower, pd_upper, ...)
line pointers: 4 bytes each, in insertion order
  offset (15 bits), flags (2 bits), length (15 bits)
free space
tuples, packed from the end of the page
special space (empty for heap pages)

row address: ctid = (page, line pointer number)

b.label: SQLite table b-tree page
b.title: page size: a power of two, 512 to 65536
b.src:
8-byte header (leaf) or 12-byte header (interior)
cell pointers: 2 bytes each, sorted in key order
unallocated space
cell content, packed from the end of the page
  holes tracked as freeblocks and 1 to 3 byte fragments

row address: the rowid key, found through the b-tree

compare.note: Both are slotted pages: pointers at the front, content at the back, free space between. The difference is what the order of the pointers means. PostgreSQL's line pointers are in the order the rows arrived, and a pointer's number is a fixed address, so indexes can point straight at it. SQLite keeps its pointers sorted by key, because each of its pages is one node of a B-tree, the sorted index that lesson 4 of this track builds. So a row's place in that array changes as other rows come and go, and SQLite finds rows by key instead.

worked.title: Read a page's state from its header

steps.say: `page_header` says `lower = 652` and `upper = 656` for an 8 KB table page. Count the line pointers: the slot array runs from the end of the 24-byte header to `lower`, at 4 bytes per pointer.
Find the free space: it's the gap between the two offsets.
Find the average row size. The rows fill everything from `upper` to the end of the page, because the special area is empty (`special = 8192`).
steps.code:
row bytes = 8192 - upper = 7536
per row   = 7536 / 157 = 48 bytes

steps.say: Decide whether one more 48-byte row fits. It needs its bytes plus a new line pointer, and only 4 bytes are free, so this page is full, and the free space map sends the next insert elsewhere. Here's the same check in the lab's page:

lab.title: Build a slotted page
steps: Open `SlottedPage.kt`. The helpers at the bottom for the header and the slots (`lower`, `upper`, `slotOffset`, `slotLength`, `setSlot`) are done. Use them instead of raw positions in the buffer.
Run the tests once. All 10 fail.
Write `freeSpace` (one line) and `get` (a length of 0 means a dead slot; check that the slot number exists).
Write `insert`: reject empty and too-large records, then place the record right below `upper`, add its slot at `slotCount()`, and move `lower` and `upper`.
Write `delete` (mark the slot dead) and `compact` (slide live records to the end of the page, then update their offsets and `upper`).
Make `insert` call `compact` when the holes would make room. Run the tests until all 10 pass.
hints: Free space after a compaction is `PAGE_SIZE - lower - (sum of live record lengths)`. Compare that with `record.size + SLOT_SIZE` to choose between compacting and returning null.

In `compact`, handle live records from the highest offset down (the one closest to the end first). Each one then moves only into space that's already free, and `System.arraycopy` on `buf.array()` is safe even when the source and the target overlap.
`buf.put(index, bytes)` and `buf.get(index, bytes)` copy at a fixed position; they don't move the buffer's own position.
The layout test reads the raw bytes: `lower` at offset 0, `upper` at offset 2, slot 0 at offset 4. If it fails while the others pass, check that the first record ends exactly at byte 4096.

drill.title: Write insert and compact from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Using only the helpers `lower`, `upper`, `slotOffset`, `slotLength`, `setSlot` and `slotCount`, write `insert` for a slotted page (compacting when the holes help) and `compact`. Then check: does a record keep its slot number through `compact`?

recap: A PostgreSQL table is a heap: a file of 8 KB pages, with rows wherever there's room. The free space map points each insert at a page with room.
A slotted page keeps a header, an array of slots (line pointers) that grows from the front, and rows packed from the back. Free space is the gap between `pd_lower` and `pd_upper`.
A row's address is (page, slot). The slot number stays fixed while the row lives, so a page can move its bytes without breaking indexes.
DELETE leaves the row in place with `t_xmax` set. VACUUM frees the slot and tidies the page, but the file doesn't shrink: the space goes to new rows.
Each row costs a 24-byte header plus a 4-byte line pointer. Rows wider than about 2 KB get compressed, or have big values moved to a TOAST table in chunks of about 2,000 bytes.
The limit: a heap keeps rows in no order, so finding one row by a value means reading every page, until an index points straight at its address.
closing:
We started with a team that deleted a year of payments and found the table's file the same size, to the byte. A delete only marks the row. VACUUM makes its space reusable inside the file, and the file shrinks only when whole pages at its end are empty.

On any PostgreSQL database you can reach, run `SELECT ctid, * FROM ledger LIMIT 5;` (any table will do) to see each row's address. Delete a row, run VACUUM, and check which addresses stay the same.

Next, we'll keep the pages that queries read again and again in memory, and find out how a database chooses which page to throw out when memory is full.

quiz.q: Every row in a table is 120 bytes, counting its 24-byte header. About how many rows fit on one 8 KB PostgreSQL page?
quiz.why: The page has a 24-byte header, and each row needs its 120 bytes plus a 4-byte line pointer: (8192 - 24) / 124 = 65.9, so 65. 68 forgets the line pointers (8168 / 120). 85 counts only the 96 bytes of column data, and forgets that every row carries its own header.

quiz.q: An index entry points at (page 12, slot 7). VACUUM then tidies page 12, and the row in slot 7 moves 300 bytes. What happens on the next lookup through the index?
options: The lookup fails until the index is rebuilt
VACUUM changed the index entry to the row's new byte offset
The lookup reads slot 7, which now holds the row's new offset, and finds the row
The row was moved to a new page, so the lookup follows a note left behind
quiz.why: Indexes never store byte offsets, only (page, slot). Tidying moves the bytes and updates the slot's offset, so the same index entry keeps working, and nobody touches the index at all. That extra step through the slot is the reason slotted pages exist.

quiz.q: Your lab page has 36 bytes of free space in one piece and 300 bytes in holes left by deleted records. What should `insert` do with a 250-byte record?
options: Return null, because only 36 bytes are free
Put the record into the biggest hole
Reuse the slot of one of the deleted records
Compact the page first, then insert into the single 336-byte gap
quiz.why: The record needs 254 bytes (250 plus a 4-byte slot). After compaction the free gap is 36 + 300 = 336 bytes, so it fits. A record can't be split across holes, and reusing a dead slot number would let an old index entry find the wrong record.

quiz.q: Each row of a payments table stores the bank's full reply as `text`, about 50 KB that barely compresses. What does the row on the page hold for that column?
options: An 18-byte pointer to chunks of about 2,000 bytes in the table's TOAST table
The full 50 KB, spread across seven pages in a row
Nothing: PostgreSQL refuses rows bigger than one page
The first 2 KB of the text, with the rest in the WAL
quiz.why: A row must fit in one page, so PostgreSQL compresses wide values and, if the row is still over about 2 KB, moves them out into the TOAST table and leaves an 18-byte pointer. Rows never stretch across pages. And the WAL is a log of changes, not a place to keep column values.

quiz.q: From Bytes, pages and durability: a payment is inserted, PostgreSQL appends the change to its write-ahead log (the WAL), and COMMIT returns. The 8 KB page with the new row is still only in memory when the server crashes. Is the row there after the restart?
options: No, because the page was never written to the drive
Yes, because recovery replays the WAL and makes the insert on the page again
Only if a checkpoint had finished after the commit
Only if the table has a primary key
quiz.why: COMMIT returns only after the WAL up to the commit record has been forced to the drive. On restart, recovery replays WAL records from the last checkpoint and applies the insert to the page again. That's why the database doesn't need to write table pages at commit time. The first option is the tempting one for anyone who thinks the table file is the only copy.

flashcards.front: What is a ctid in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: A row's address: (page number, line pointer number). Indexes store it.

flashcards.front: What do `pd_lower` and `pd_upper` mark on a page?
flashcards.back: `pd_lower` is the end of the line pointer array; `pd_upper` is the start of the row data. The free space is between them.

flashcards.front: Why can a page move its rows without breaking indexes?
flashcards.back: Indexes point at (page, slot). Tidying moves the bytes and updates the slot's offset, so the slot number stays the same.

flashcards.front: What does a PostgreSQL DELETE do to the row on the page?
flashcards.back: It leaves the bytes where they are and sets the row's `t_xmax` to the deleting transaction's id. VACUUM makes the space reusable later.

flashcards.front: How big is a PostgreSQL row header, and what does a line pointer cost?
flashcards.back: 23 bytes, padded to 24 when the row has no empty (NULL) values. Each row also needs a 4-byte line pointer.

flashcards.front: When does TOAST start, and what is left in the row?
flashcards.back: When a row is wider than about 2 KB. Big values are compressed and, if still too big, moved to the TOAST table in chunks of about 2,000 bytes; the row keeps an 18-byte pointer.

terms.plain: The fixed-size block (8 KB in PostgreSQL) that a database reads, writes and caches as one piece.
A table file whose rows sit wherever there's room, in no order.
A page with an array of slots at the front that point to rows of any length packed at the back.
PostgreSQL's 4-byte slot: where the row starts, how long it is, and its state.
A PostgreSQL row's address: (page, line pointer number).
A small side file that records roughly how much room each page has, so an insert can find one quickly.
PostgreSQL's cleanup command: it frees the slots of dead rows and makes their space reusable inside the file.
PostgreSQL's way of storing big column values compressed, or out of the row in a separate table.

explain_back.prompt: A friend asks why a PostgreSQL page keeps an array of line pointers instead of packing rows one after another. Explain it to them, and say what would break if VACUUM renumbered the rows after tidying a page.
explain_back.answer: Rows have different lengths, so you can't find row 4 by multiplying 4 by a row size. The line pointer array gives each row a slot of fixed size that holds where the row starts and how long it is. Indexes store (page, slot), never a byte position. So the page can move row bytes around, for example when VACUUM closes the holes left by deleted rows, as long as it updates the slot. If VACUUM renumbered the rows instead, every index entry pointing at that page would suddenly point at the wrong row, or at nothing. The database would have to rewrite its indexes every time it tidied a page.

deeper.body:
**Line pointer states.** `lp_flags` has four values: 0 unused, 1 normal, 2 redirect, 3 dead. You saw 0 and 1. A dead pointer (3) has lost its row but may still be pointed at by index entries, so it can't be reused yet. A redirect (2) appears with **HOT updates** (heap-only tuples). When an UPDATE, the SQL command that changes a row, changes no column that an index covers, and the new version fits on the same page, PostgreSQL writes the new version on that page and adds no new index entries. Later, when PostgreSQL tidies the page, the old version's pointer becomes a redirect to the new one, so the index entry still leads to the live row. HOT updates are much cheaper than ordinary ones, which must add an entry to every index.

**fillfactor.** For tables, the default `fillfactor` is 100: inserts pack pages full. A table whose rows change all the time, say a balance row rewritten on every payment, can be created `WITH (fillfactor = 80)`, so each page keeps 20% free for HOT updates. You trade disk space for fewer index writes.

**Oracle does the same.** An Oracle data block (8 KB by default on most systems) has a block header, a row directory and row data that fills from the bottom up. A ROWID, Oracle's row address, holds the row's slot number inside its block, much like a ctid.

**Where the lab and PostgreSQL part ways.** The lab's page compacts whenever an insert needs the room. PostgreSQL tidies a table page when a query visits it and finds it nearly full, and during VACUUM. To move row bytes it needs a cleanup lock: an exclusive lock, held while it's the only process using the page. Another process could be holding a pointer straight into the page's memory, and moving bytes under it would make it read the wrong row. That rule belongs to the buffer pool, which is the next lesson.
